From long time I am a member of IMDb but I never try write a review. But in this case I can not ignore writing review option.The screenplay was written by Frank Darabont, who based it on the novella "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption" by Stephen King. He adapts the material so well that he really transcends it, turning the film into a work of art. Many avid readers will claim the book is always better than the movie, but that is simply not the case here. King is a tremendous writer, but even he can't shade and color the prison the way that Darabont does, which sets the mood for the entire film. The characters King created in the book are deeper and more well drawn in the film in large part because of Darabont's script.Many moviegoers turn their noses up at the thought of a movie about the triumph of the human spirit. However, even those jaded film fans will love "The Shawshank Redemption" because it sets a new standard for films in this genre. It is an unapologetically emotional and sometimes sentimental take on friendship and life, even when that life is spent in a cage, and will make viewers laugh, cry, and reflect on their own lives in ways that very few movies can. It may not have won a single Oscar, but it will win your heart, and perhaps that is more important.

review_title: A Timeless Story of Hope and Friendship
review_text: The Shawshank Redemption is one of those rare films that touches the soul. It tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a man wrongly imprisoned, who never gives up hope and slowly transforms the lives of those around him. Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman deliver phenomenal performances, supported by a thoughtful script, beautiful cinematography, and an unforgettable score. It's not just a prison drama-it's a profound reflection on resilience, friendship, and the human spirit. Every rewatch reveals new layers of meaning, and the emotional payoff is as strong as ever. A true cinematic masterpiece that only gets better with time.

Review from Roger Ebert: There are key moments in the film, as when Andy uses his clout to get some cold beers for his friends who are working on a roofing job. Or when he befriends the old prison librarian (James Whitmore). Or when he oversteps his boundaries and is thrown into solitary confinement. What quietly amazes everyone in the prison -- and us, too -- is the way he accepts the good and the bad as all part of some larger pattern than only he can fully see.The partnership between the characters played by Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman is crucial to the way the story unfolds. This is not a "prison drama" in any conventional sense of the word. It is not about violence, riots or melodrama. The word "redemption" is in the title for a reason. The movie is based on a story, Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption, by Stephen King, which is quite unlike most of King's work. The horror here is not of the supernatural kind, but of the sort that flows from the realization than 10, 20, 30 years of a man's life have unreeled in the same unchanging daily prison routine.

I enjoyed this movie, but I still regard it as one of the most vastly over-rated films of all time. The villains in the film were 2-dimensional caricatures. There were no shades of gray in this film whatsoever. I can accept such villains when some element of the fairy tale, some element of the supernatural is introduced. For instance, it was okay for Chigurh to be cartoonish in No Country For Old Men because he was clearly supposed to be a symbol, a force of nature. The warden in Shawshank Redemption, on the other hand, isn't a force of nature, merely a poorly-written character.Honestly, the Shawshank Redemption was absorbing, but it wasn't a "great film" (in the capital-letters sense) by any stretch of the imagination.

My fascination with Shawshank lies in the fact that it was written by Stephen King.There is no doubt that King is one of the world's best writers. Some of the greatest stories ever told have been found in books such as IT and the Castle Rock series. Nevertheless, the best directors are always responsible for his best adaptations. Kubrick interpreted The Shining beautifully, and Rob Reiner directed Misery and Stand By Me as well. As a result, Frank Darabont made one of the best King films ever made. King's message is clearly understood by him, and he conveys it beautifully through his writing.Among the best films ever made, this one demonstrates a powerful message. Hope is eternal in it. Despite not committing a crime, Tim Robbins' Andy Dufresne is sent to prison for one. Despite this, he never gives up hope. No matter how hard he tries, he never gives up on his quest for freedom. With years of tenacity, patience, and wit, he has not only kept himself sane, but he has given his mind and spirit a will to live. The film has a unique feel. There is a lot of life and humor in it, and warmth in the friendship that builds up between Andy and Red. There is even excitement and suspense, although not when we expect it. review_title: My favorite movie of all time.
review_text: "The Shawshank Redemption," based on the novel by Stephen King, was masterfully directed by Frank Darabont. Adapting a book to the big screen is no easy feat, especially when the source material is as beloved as this one. However, Darabont's work not only stays true to the book, but also stands on its own as a brilliant film. One of the standout performances in the movie is Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, which adds a new and powerful dimension to the character. Red's friendship with the protagonist, Andy Dufresne (played by Tim Robbins), adds depth and complexity to the story. Andy's journey is captivating and keeps the viewer engaged throughout the entire film. The fact that Andy is a flawed and complex protagonist only adds to the compelling nature of the story. Additionally, the lack of two-dimensional villains, aside from The Sisters, gives the audience more reasons to root for Andy. I also want to give a special mention to Brooks, whose character arc is heart-wrenching and adds to the emotional impact of the film. Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a must-see movie that offers hope and teaches us to never give up on our dreams.

Morgan Freeman as Red brings wisdom and warmth to the character, and his narration adds an extra layer of connection.The visuals and cinematography effectively capture the emotions of the characters.The movie's music, composed by Thomas Newman, complements the story beautifully. On Sept. 23, 1994, after a premiere at the Toronto film fest, The Shawshank Redemption hit theaters nationwide. The Morgan Freeman film eventually nabbed seven Oscar nominations. The Hollywood Reporter's original review is below:Castle Rock has tapped into the wellspring of yet another Stephen King novella, from the same collection as Stand by Me. While it seems unlikely that this well-wrought film about hope and friendship in a maximum security prison will do Stand by Me-level business, The Shawshank Redemption should appeal to a mature audience. The marketing challenge will be to lure a mainstream audience to this dark drama starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman with, to boot, an enigmatic title.Covering a span of time from 1946 to 1967, Shawshank focuses on the plight of a Maine banker, Andy Dufresne (Robbins), sentenced to two life terms for the murder of his wife and lover. Laconic and a bit chilly, Andy is somewhat of an outcast among the uneducated, macho thugs who make up the main brunt of the prison population.Admittedly, he's not an easy guy to get to know and only comes to enjoy a prison friendship when he makes a deal with the prison black-market supplier, Red (Freeman), to get him a tiny hammer for his rock collection. Red is also an enigma to most of the inmates. He keeps his nose clean and his hopes up even though the parole board routinely denies him pardon, obviously a racial antagonism.While the story roils with some rousing prison-type action and is coarsened by an overpowering sense of frustration, The Shawshank Redemption is really about the unlikely friendship between Andy and Red: Each nurtures the other and serves as a touchstone for keeping their sanity intact.Frank Darabont's writing and direction are generally crisp, but Shawshank is a tough watch and audiences could use some time cut from its 142 minutes.

**Review: *Shawshank Redemption* (1994)**While *The Shawshank Redemption* isn't typically categorized as an "action movie" in the traditional sense-lacking car chases, explosive gunfights, and larger-than-life set pieces-it possesses a kind of action that is no less riveting: the action of the human spirit fighting against the oppressive weight of despair and injustice. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella *Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption*, the film stands as a testament to perseverance, hope, and the unbreakable bonds of friendship, making it one of the most profound and enduring films in cinematic history.The story follows Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker wrongly convicted of his wife's murder, as he spends years imprisoned at Shawshank State Penitentiary. His transformation from a man broken by the system to one who transcends it is the heart of the film, and his unlikely friendship with Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman) anchors the narrative. While the film has all the trappings of a prison drama-gritty surroundings, harsh conditions, corrupt officials-it also carries a quiet tension, with each scene building toward the ultimate act of redemption.The film's pacing is deliberate, allowing its characters to unfold organically. Andy, played with a quiet intensity by Robbins, is initially distant and reserved. But as the film progresses, we see him become an unintentional leader within Shawshank, earning the respect of both the inmates and the prison's corrupt warden (a chillingly cold Bob Gunton). Andy's financial expertise leads to him managing the warden's illicit operations, but it is his passion for education and his love of hope that makes him a beacon of light in an otherwise dark and brutal environment.Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is nothing short of iconic. Freeman's deep, gravelly voice lends gravitas to Red's narration, providing a philosophical and reflective lens through which we experience the unfolding drama. His character, a man who has spent most of his life in Shawshank, serves as the film's emotional anchor. The friendship that grows between Red and Andy is tender and real, a testament to the power of human connection in the face of systemic dehumanization. Freeman's performance is filled with layers of emotion, from the humor of his parole hearings to the profound sadness of a man who has long since given up hope, only to rediscover it through Andy's unwavering belief in a better future.While *The Shawshank Redemption* may not boast the traditional action movie elements, it offers something arguably more powerful: a battle of wills. The "action" is in the small victories-Andy's creation of a library, his daring escape through a tunnel of hope, the final payoff of a meticulously planned redemption. Each of these moments, while quieter than typical action scenes, is earned through years of emotional buildup.The film's direction and cinematography by Roger Deakins deserve special mention. Shawshank Penitentiary itself becomes a character in the film, its oppressive walls and cold, institutional design mirroring the internal struggles of its inhabitants. The score by Thomas Newman adds to the film's mood, with its subtle, haunting melodies underscoring the moments of introspection and triumph.At its core, *The Shawshank Redemption* is a movie about the power of perseverance, hope, and friendship in the face of impossible odds. While it may not fit the conventional mold of an action film, it delivers a kind of action that resonates far deeper-one that speaks to the resilience of the human spirit.

The film shows how even in the darkest of places, there is always a glimmer of hope that can help people survive and even thrive. The relationship between Andy and Red is a perfect example of this, as they help each other through the struggles of life behind bars.The film also features outstanding performances from its cast, especially Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman. Robbins delivers a nuanced portrayal of Andy, showing both his vulnerability and his resilience. Freeman, meanwhile, brings warmth and humanity to his role as Red, making him a character that audiences root for from start to finish. In terms of technical aspects, the cinematography, editing, and score of "The Shawshank Redemption" are all top-notch. The film's use of voice-over narration from Red adds an extra layer of depth to the story and helps to highlight the film's themes of hope and redemption.Overall, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterpiece that deserves all the praise it has received over the years. It's a film that can make audiences laugh, cry, and feel inspired all at once, and it's a testament to the power of cinema to tell stories that resonate with people for decades to come.

The climactic twist is both satisfying and uplifting, leaving a lasting impression long after the credits roll.However, the film isn't without its minor flaws. review_text: Released in 1994 and directed by Frank Darabont, "The Shawshank Redemption" stands tall as an everlasting masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences with its powerful storytelling, brilliant performances, and profound themes. Adapted from Stephen King's novella, this film effortlessly weaves a tale of hope, friendship, and redemption, leaving an indelible mark on the annals of cinema."The Shawshank Redemption" takes place within the confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary, where Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a falsely accused banker, finds himself serving a life sentence. As Andy navigates the harsh realities of prison life, he forges an unlikely friendship with Red (Morgan Freeman), a seasoned inmate known for his resourcefulness and wisdom. Together, they embark on a journey that challenges the limitations of their circumstances and explores the depths of the human spirit.One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its exceptional storytelling. Frank Darabont's screenplay strikes a perfect balance between tension, drama, and heartfelt moments, ensuring that every scene serves a purpose in advancing the narrative. The pacing is deliberate, allowing the characters to develop organically and the emotional weight of their experiences to resonate deeply with the audience. Each twist and turn in the plot is executed with precision, keeping viewers on the edge of their seats and emotionally invested until the very end.The performances in "The Shawshank Redemption" are nothing short of extraordinary. Tim Robbins delivers a tour de force performance as Andy Dufresne, capturing the character's resilience, intelligence, and quiet determination with finesse. His transformation over the course of the film is both believable and inspiring. Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red is a career-defining role, as he effortlessly exudes warmth, wisdom, and empathy. Freeman's narration, with his distinctive voice, adds an additional layer of depth to the storytelling, drawing audiences further into the narrative.The supporting cast is equally commendable, with memorable performances from Bob Gunton as the ruthless prison warden Samuel Norton, and William Sadler as the tragic Brooks Hatlen. Each actor brings a distinct presence to their roles, adding depth and complexity to the ensemble. Their performances serve as a testament to the film's casting choices and the talent involved.Visually, "The Shawshank Redemption" captures the starkness and claustrophobia of prison life, juxtaposing it with moments of breathtaking beauty. The cinematography by Roger Deakins is masterful, utilizing lighting, composition, and framing to convey the emotional tone of each scene. The film's color palette ranges from muted and desaturated tones within the prison walls to vibrant hues symbolizing hope and freedom. This visual juxtaposition reinforces the central themes of the story and enhances the overall viewing experience.The musical score composed by Thomas Newman is evocative and adds another layer of emotional depth to the film. It seamlessly blends with the narrative, accentuating key moments and heightening the viewer's emotional response. From poignant piano melodies to stirring orchestral arrangements, the music perfectly complements the film's themes and elevates the storytelling."The Shawshank Redemption" transcends its prison setting and becomes a universal tale of the resilience of the human spirit. It explores profound themes of hope, friendship, and the pursuit of freedom, reminding us of the inherent capacity for redemption within each individual. The film's enduring message continues to resonate with audiences, prompting introspection and inspiring a renewed belief in the power of hope and the strength of the human will.In conclusion, "The Shawshank Redemption" is an unparalleled cinematic masterpiece that deserves its place among the greatest films ever made.

From the poignant scenes of camaraderie among the inmates to the exhilarating moments of Andy's secretive endeavors, "The Shawshank Redemption" keeps audiences engaged and invested in the characters' fates. The screenplay is rich with memorable lines and profound themes, exploring the concepts of freedom, justice, and the enduring power of hope.The cinematography by Roger Deakins is visually stunning, capturing the stark contrast between the drab prison environment and the moments of beauty and liberation. Thomas Newman's hauntingly beautiful score further enhances the film's emotional depth, perfectly complementing its narrative arc."The Shawshank Redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that resonates with viewers on a deeply personal level. It is a testament to the human spirit's ability to persevere against all odds and find redemption even in the darkest of places. This film is not just a story of one man's journey, but a universal tale of hope and the transformative power of friendship. The future is something no one can predict, but one thing is undeniable, this movie has lit up many broken and desperate souls out there, that is the power of The Shawshank Redemption, you will only be able to understand and feel the full message if the life you are living is experiencing something, a certain condition.Andy Dufresne is probably a very good character, full of positivity, a strong desire for freedom. He's smart, hard-working, persistent, but naive enough to believe Norton will let him go when Tommy reveals the truth. This contrasts with Brooks. I'm not saying Brooks is a character filled with negativity, he's simply not as lucky as Red. It can be said that Andy is Red's hope. review_title: Everything a movie should be and more
review_text: I am not a writer, consequently any review I might make will not capture the essence of what I wanted to articulate. Therefore instead of a review, I'll give a statement regarding this film: This is one of the few times where a film's success, it's overall feeling and merits, surpasses that of the book (or in this case story), and in stating this, there should be no diminution to what Stephen King wrote.In regards to books being made into films, I feel that each version (film and story) itself enhances the other, and each should not be compared or critiqued for what is lacking, or plentiful. Instead, they should each be looked upon as a separate entity, with each 'form' evoking our emotions in their own unique and separate way!In order to make these statements, I have to say that I have read the Stephen King short story (or novella), "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption". I have also listened to the audio-book, and all three inspire, give hope and yes even define the word 'Redemption', in their own unique ways.One might not be able to fairly compare an apple's flavour, to that of an orange, but you certainly can compare a Granny Smith to a Red Delicious. They are both apples at the core, it's the texture, pulp and flavour that make it different. That core could be a story, and each medium (written, visual, audio etc) provides a similar, yet unique flavour to be savored!

review_title: Not Number 1 Material, But Still Good
review_text: I break my reviewing of movies down into five aspects, each worth two stars, plot, characters, cinematography, soundtrack, and acting. So here's my broken down review of Shawshank Redemption: Plot: One star. While the plot flows neatly, is well developed, and doesn't have any loopholes I noticed, it lacks the originality one would expect from the top rated movie on IMDb. I have no complaints other than the lack of providing me with something truly original and complex. It's not a simple plot, per say, just as it's not an unoriginal plot, but it is by no means an extremely original or complex plot.Characters: Two stars. No characters went blatantly against psychology, nor did they ever break their characterization. Characterization was pretty good and I have no real complaints, all I would have to question is Andy's character. He was gang raped and got his ass kicked multiple times and was still this calm, cool, collected guy. I don't see how that would work out in the real world, so I didn't find that really believable, but he kept with his characterization and the movie made up for it with the almost relatable nature of Red's character and how well the minor characters were developed. That's probably what blew me away character-wise. No character was exceptionally complex, but all stayed true to their characterization. However, Andy should have been more complex than he was, seeing as how he was the main character.Cinematography: Two stars. I have no complaints. Camera angles, effects, etc. were very good, though there was nothing exceptional about them that really stood out to me. Though I do realize that it was pretty well done for a 90's movie. Again, no complaints.Soundtrack: Two stars. Again, very well done, no complaints here. At no time did it overshadow dialogue, and at no time were there awkward silences. However, nothing really stood out to me. Not a soundtrack I'd go on raving to my friends about, but no complaints.Acting: One star. This is obviously unexpected. I mean, Morgan Freeman and Tim Robbins...I was surprised I didn't find it amazing. But Morgan Freeman's monologues lacked heart and Tim Robbins' character didn't give him any room for heart to be placed into it. Again, the best acting in the movie, in my opinion, would be from the minor characters. Frank Medrano is worth note, in my opinion, as he was very, very good. But he didn't remain in the movie long, so him and the other minor characters didn't make it enough for me to give acting two stars. I'm sure many people would disagree, though.All in all, I give this movie eight stars and would recommend it to a friend, but I wouldn't have it rated first on IMDb because, while it was very good, it didn't strike me as THAT good. There are more original movies out there that I would recommend before this, though I do recommend that people watch this movie along with the others.

Shawkshank RedemptionThat name, Shawshank Redemption, has always been around since I was born. I never really understood why everyone watched and spoke of great things about that movie until now. After watching Shawshank Redemption, it really opened my mind to a lot of different things. This movie not only provided, the drama and crime, but it also provided action and even a mystery. This movie is about a man who had a successful career as a banker; however, one day he came home to find out that his wife was having an affair with him. In anger he decided to pull out a revolver and fix the problem himself. So later on he is then accused of first-degree murder and sentenced to two life terms in prison. While in prison the banker had a series of obstacles he had to overcome, especially being a rich guy who had everything he wanted to be a convict who is stripped away from their life. After a few years in Shawshank Prison, the banker finally began to get acclimated. Later on, it did not take long for the banker to hear that he may be innocent and then try to devise a plan to show his innocence that just may or may not work. The main characters in this film were played as, Morgan Freeman and Tim Robbins; thus in my opinion, were outstanding actors and really portrayed their characters as if it were them living that life. I believe that the director of this film did a great job in producing such an awesome movie. This review is actually very hard to write because there is so many emotions I feel after watching the movie. How be ever, the movie offered a great deal of implied metaphors such as when Morgan Freeman uses slang to describe his feelings towards other inmates which allowed the audience to constantly sit on the edge of their seat not knowing what might happen next. This movie may not be your modern era film, but it definitely made an impact on the reality of life. The director, Frank Darabont, definitely put a lot of emphasis on how Tim Robbins' character was influenced by others throughout the movie. Same goes with Morgan Freeman, his character in this movie impacted a lot of people either in a negative way or even a positive way.In Shawshank Redemption, I think by the setting taken place in a prison really presented a more "harsh times" feel to the movie such as sexual harassment and brutal beatings by guards. Also I really enjoyed how every little phrase or word, both by an inmate or a guard, stood out and brought a different meaning to the movie. When you watch this movie you must pay attention to every little detail. If you don't, then you will be lost and continue to ask yourself, "What is going on?" That's just how it is with Shawshank Redemption. In this movie you would think it would be just your average prison film but it's not. I would recommend this movie to anyone that is interested in a good mystery/action and even a drama. This is an outstanding movie and I'm so glad I watched it because it definitely opened my mind about the reality of life's struggles.

Released in 1994 and directed by Frank Darabont, this film is a powerful testament to the resilience of the human spirit and the enduring nature of hope.Adapted from Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," the film revolves around the life of Andy Dufresne, a banker who is wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife and her lover. Set within the confines of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the narrative unfolds as a poignant exploration of friendship, redemption, and the unwavering belief in one's humanity.At the heart of the film is the remarkable portrayal of characters by Tim Robbins as Andy Dufresne and Morgan Freeman as Ellis "Red" Redding. Robbins captures the essence of Andy's quiet strength and determination, while Freeman's narration lends a poetic and reflective quality to the story. Their on-screen chemistry is nothing short of brilliant, forming the backbone of the film's emotional resonance.The cinematography by Roger Deakins is visually arresting, capturing the harsh reality of prison life while infusing moments of beauty and symbolism. The iconic scene of Andy's escape through the sewage pipe, set against the backdrop of a thunderstorm, is a testament to the film's visual prowess.

What have we become, if not a nation of lost beings? We seem to be starving from the ravages of unmet needs and relentless fear-- festering deeply a growing malnutrition of the soul. Indeed, was there ever a time when human beings truly lived to the full measure of their capacity for good?Every once in a while a story is so beautifully constructed that we find a penetrating transformation has overtaken us, defying explanation, yet is as instinctively recognizable as joy, or laughter, or even deep sorrow. Such is the work of Writer/Director Frank Darabont in his powerful motion picture tale, "The Shawshank Redemption", which is based on a most unassuming parable by Stephen King.Only through redemption will our nation find its way; and it is only by the people, those individuals who refuse to compromise their capacity to create beauty--or better, recognize it--who will guide us to our true potential as a society, or more fundamentally, as a planetary species.Indeed, beyond redemption is a lighted pathway to our intended destiny, where fear transforms into compassion and hope becomes the new reality, ever nourishing our spirit.Remember how you felt after watching this film? Though it may be true that we have never met, in many ways I know who you are. And with that insight wells up a comfort so luminous it lights this pathway on which, through all the mysteriousness of the vast universe, we both travel ever onward and upward.Ellison Horne

"The Shawshank Redemption" is more than just a film; it's a cinematic experience that leaves an indelible mark on its audience. Directed by Frank Darabont and based on Stephen King's novella "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption," this film stands as a testament to the power of hope and friendship in the face of adversity.The story follows Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, as he navigates life within the oppressive walls of Shawshank State Penitentiary. His journey is one of resilience and quiet determination, punctuated by his unlikely friendship with Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), a long-time inmate and the film's narrator. Freeman's voiceover adds a layer of poignancy and introspection, guiding the audience through the narrative with wisdom and warmth.What sets "The Shawshank Redemption" apart is its deep, humanistic storytelling. The film delves into themes of hope, redemption, and the enduring human spirit, all while maintaining a gripping and emotionally engaging plot. The character development is exceptional, with Robbins and Freeman delivering performances that are both powerful and nuanced. The chemistry between the two leads is palpable, making their friendship feel authentic and deeply moving.The supporting cast also shines, with standout performances from Bob Gunton as the corrupt warden, Samuel Norton, and Clancy Brown as the brutal prison guard, Captain Hadley. Each character adds depth to the story, creating a rich tapestry of life within Shawshank.Visually, the film is stunning. Roger Deakins' cinematography captures the bleakness of prison life while also highlighting moments of beauty and serenity, such as the iconic rooftop scene where Andy and his fellow inmates enjoy a brief taste of freedom. Thomas Newman's haunting score further elevates the film, perfectly complementing its emotional beats."The Shawshank Redemption" is a masterclass in filmmaking, storytelling, and acting. It's a film that resonates on a profound level, reminding us of the importance of hope and the human capacity for endurance. Whether you're watching it for the first time or the tenth, it never fails to inspire and move.

His journey of self-discovery and friendship with fellow inmate Ellis "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman) is the heart and soul of the movie. Through their eyes, we are shown a world where friendship blooms in the harshest conditions, and hope becomes an act of defiance.As the prison walls close in on the inmates, the film's cinematography takes our breath away. The sweeping shots of the imposing penitentiary and the iconic scene of Andy standing triumphant in the rain will forever be etched in our collective memory. The movie paints a vivid portrait of the inescapable human condition; our laughter is juxtaposed with heart-wrenching tears, and our fears are confronted by the resolute power of hope.But what truly sets "The Shawshank Redemption" apart is its mastery of storytelling. The narrative is at once a riveting tale of camaraderie and an allegory of the human spirit's resilience. With every seemingly inconsequential detail weaved into the fabric of the story, Darabont brings King's novella to life with a finesse that leaves the audience spellbound. The movie's dramatic crescendo - the masterful escape of Andy - is a cinematic tour de force, an exhilarating testament to the power of hope and determination.The ensemble cast is nothing short of extraordinary, led by Robbins and Freeman, who infuse their characters with quiet dignity and raw vulnerability. Their performances are imbued with grace and gravitas, making their friendship a beacon of light in the abyss of despair. The supporting cast, including Bob Gunton as the merciless Warden Norton and Clancy Brown as the brutal Captain Hadley, offers a compelling portrayal of the darker side of human nature.As the end credits roll, one cannot help but be left awestruck by the film's hauntingly beautiful score, composed by Thomas Newman. His melodies linger long after the screen fades to black, serving as a poignant reminder of the emotional odyssey we have just witnessed.In the pantheon of great cinema, "The Shawshank Redemption" stands proud as an enduring testament to the power of friendship and the unyielding resilience of the human spirit. It is a story that transcends time and space, a tale of redemption that reaches into the very depths of our souls. review_title: Beneath the surface of cinematic worship
review_text: "The Shawshank Redemption" by Frank Darabont is one of those films that often gets elevated to the heights of cinema as an undisputed masterpiece. But sometimes, digging deeper, one realizes that behind the veil of cinematic worship lie imperfections that deserve examination. The plot of the film follows the story of Andy Dufresne, portrayed by Tim Robbins, a man unjustly convicted of a crime he did not commit. Set in the harsh reality of Shawshank State Penitentiary, the film explores his quest for freedom, not just physical but also mental, through resilience and hope. One of the film's weaknesses is its predictability. From the opening scenes, one can easily anticipate the path the protagonist will take to achieve redemption. This lack of suspense and surprise makes some scenes less engaging than they could be, diminishing the overall emotional impact of the film. Moreover, "The Shawshank Redemption" suffers from an excess of sentimentality that can sometimes feel cloying. The relationships between characters are often depicted in a melodramatic manner, with dialogues that tend to artificially tug at the heartstrings. This excess of sentimentality can detract from the film's deeper message. Another critical aspect is the lack of thematic depth. Despite addressing important themes such as redemption and human resilience, the film approaches them superficially, without fully exploring the complexities and nuances of these concepts. Prison life is portrayed in a stereotypical manner, failing to fully capture the brutality and harshness of such an environment. Despite these flaws, there are still positive aspects to acknowledge. The performances of the main actors are impeccable and add depth to the characters. Particularly, Morgan Freeman in the role of Ellis Redding delivers a memorable performance that lingers in the viewer's memory. Furthermore, Darabont's direction successfully captures the claustrophobic atmosphere of the prison, creating some memorable scenes that prompt reflection on the meaning of freedom and hope. The final verdict on "The Shawshank Redemption" cannot ignore its qualities and flaws. While the film is widely appreciated for some of its aspects, it's important to recognize that it is not immune to valid criticism. The predictability of the plot, the excess of sentimentality, and the lack of thematic depth are aspects that require critical and mindful analysis from the viewer. Despite offering moments of great emotional impact and high-level performances, the film falls short of the excellence it is sometimes attributed. Ultimately, "The Shawshank Redemption" is a work that, despite its merits, requires careful and balanced examination to be fully appreciated.

review_title: A very good movie, but overrated nonetheless.
review_text: The Shawshank Redemption was released in a very good year for movies (1994) and although it could very well be argued that, at the time, it did not get the credit it deserved-- being overshadowed by movies like Pulp Fiction and Forrest Gump, it now may get more credit than it is due. Time and time again I have heard the phrase, "They don't make them like this anymore," when The Shawshank Redemption is spoke of. However, it should be noted that Shawshank was not the first movie of its kind and owes much credit to its predecessors (taking elements and ideas from movies like Dead Man Walking, It's a Wonderful Life, etc.) Well paced and often times very moving, The Shawshank Redemption provides us with what is initially a very realistic situation: middle aged man Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is put on trial wrongfully (as far as we know) for murder. Found guilty, he is put in jail for a life sentence. As the movie progresses , in part from beautiful cinematography, and in part from lightly tugging at the audiences heart strings, we are able to sympathize with the inmates, and almost pity them. The concept of having a home and not knowing what to do when not in your comfort zone is something that the Shawshank Redemption uses to make a simple idea into a very good full length movie. However, it is ranked #2 on IMDb's top 250 (with a rating of 9.2 it is actually higher than The Godfather, thus should be ranked #1) and this, I believe at least, is an undeserving spot for The Shawshank Redemption. While it is very good, it is certainly not among the ranks of Citizen Kane, The Godfather and others on that level. Providing us with little or no historical or cultural relevance, the movie likely earns its ranking because people can identify with it, so they end up enjoying it, and end up giving it a 10 out of 10 because they enjoy it so much. Though it pains me to say it, just because a movie is highly enjoyable, it does not make it great by any means. Andy Dufresne acts as a metaphor for the rest of the human race, and shows, how sometimes, we are all wrongfully accused of something or other. However, the movie pertains only to itself, not taking on anything bigger-- so it stays a very good movie rather than an excellent one.

review_title: A Humble Review of the Awesome Film: A Shawshank Redemption
review_text: Suphie W. 9/13/2012The Shawshank Redemption Movie Review Though I haven't seen this film since the year of 2004, (it came out in 1994), I seriously remember being moved by it. I remember, quite vividly and with a pleasant vibe, how moved my friend and I genuinely felt when we first watched it together. These were in the days when Blockbuster was still around and when it was more monetarily feasible as well as logical to go out to your local movie store and rent a movie to watch with your friend; this was, with all due respect, before the current and giant economic melt-down that we are all experiencing. So, to set the scene and mood of the period in which we watched this film for the first time, the candles were lit, and my friend and I were seated eating gummy bears, and we stayed up and watched that sucker into the wee hours of the morning, cat-sitting. The economy was better, then, for sure, we all know, but, we were having a hell of a time (now my friend is away, teaching English abroad, in Korea, soon to retire there, though; she's had enough of it, as the lifestyle and the culture were just generally getting on her nerves, and she felt she had achieved what she wanted). Well, basically, the Shawshank Redemption is all about solitary confinement in a small, insulated, but high-security prison in middle-to-Southern Ohio, set in the '50s. Morgan Freeman and his white counterpart in the film (race was a factor back then), partner up to give each other moral support and courage during a very tough time for them both. The part that struck me most about this film, though, was that Tim Robbins, or, the character played by Tim Robbins, was put into solitary confinement, where food was shoved in his little cell in an unsanitary manner, and he was treated, as the proverb or saying goes, like a dog; and where he couldn't see nor hear from anyone for a long, long time; it was verifiable torture. In addition, Morgan Freeman, who plays someone who is, like Tim Robbins, on the death row, plays your average cool-cat gentleman who was convicted for the murdering of his wife or something, but who claims he didn't do it. There are many cafeteria scenes where the two bond joyously over their own jokes and jiving, and where they eventually become better friends. Basically, the two bond over their common suffering, and help each other through their sorrow. Indeed, Bob Gunton also plays in the film, a man who plays the jail-owner, or something. He appears, in real life, to be much older than either Robbins or Freeman, born in October of 1959, and 1937, respectively. Robbins notably graduated with honors from the drama program of UCLA in 1981, then went on to do other great things, such as forming the Actor's Gang Theatre Group, which expressed radical political views as seen through a European lens. In addition, Robbins has received many dramatic awards, and continues to do sporadic work in film. Freeman, of course, is the mighty train who continues to do well in whatever he does, and is well-liked by all, really. Bob Gunton has a tendency for playing strict, militaristic, authoritarian roles when it comes to his film-work, and he plays the role in the notable movie of The Shawshank Redemption. There are several intense scenes in the movie, The Shawshank Redemption, and many of them include the showing of the intense pain of both Freeman and Robbins, as they elude their grief. Robbins, in particular can't take the pain of being "locked-up" so to speak and often shouts, screams intensely out of frustration with having no one to talk to, and out of mental and emotional pain. Morgan Freeman notably cries, which is all the more pitiful as one sees his weary countenance.

review_title: Andy has some initial difficulty adjusting to prison life, especially because many of the other prisoners think he's a snob.
review_text: It is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "The Shawshank Redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. Many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "Shawshank" slows down and looks. It uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. It is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.Interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. The film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer Ellis 'Red' Redding (Morgan Freeman). It is his voice remembering the first time he saw Andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison. People like excitement at the movies, and titles that provide it do well. Films about "redemption" are approached with great wariness; a lot of people are not thrilled by the prospect of a great film - it sounds like work. But there's a hunger for messages of hope, and when a film offers one, it's likely to have staying power even if it doesn't grab an immediate audience."The Shawshank Redemption" premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in September 1994, and opened a few weeks later. It got good reviews but did poor business (its $18 million original gross didn't cover costs; it took in only another $10 million after winning seven Oscar nominations, including best picture).

review_title: A great story, with great performances
review_text: A faithful telling of Stephen King's novelette "Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption", this movie explores a wide range of emotions without ever feeling sensational or melodramatic. It's a really good story told really well on film (unlike a lot of King adaptations).Tim Robbins is absolutely fantastic as the "fresh" inmate, radiating intelligence, courage, innocence, and mystery with equal ability. Morgan Freeman plays the wily veteran convict who forges a respectful friendship with Robbins, and since it's Freeman, you know he does a good job.There's no special effects wizardry, no furious action, no steamy romance, no clever "Pulp Fiction" banter. It takes place virtually entirely in a prison, so there isn't much distraction with location, scenery, or movement. This movie is pure story and character, which really makes you appreciate just how amazing the performances are.The movie is basically the gradual discovery of what Robbins' character is all about--what he's done, what's he's thinking, how he's going to end up. The strength of the acting, and the adherence to King's work does a superb job in making you sincerely care about the past and fate of this man.There is also a good deal of subtle philosophical elements to the movie, which doesn't hurt. Certainly the penal system as we know it is questioned, but there is also a broader view of life itself, almost in the Victor Frankl "Man's Search for Meaning" kind of way, where the strength of the human spirit is tested to the extreme. What does it take to destroy hope and happiness?There exists only a handful of movies that I'll ever rate a solid 10. This is easily one of them.

"The Shawshank Redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair. The story is narrated by "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman), who has been inside the walls of Shawshank Prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. He can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. One day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest busload of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. Red bets on a tall, lanky guy named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

One of my all time favorites. Shawshank Redemption is a very moving story about hope and the power of friendship. Out of the three genre-defining classics released in 1994, The Shawshank Redemption was the one that ended up bearing the maximum brunt. First commercially by failing to recover its budget for it debuted in theatres together with one of cinema's greatest watershed events; Pulp Fiction. And then at Academy Awards where it was nominated for seven Oscars yet failed to win any, thanks to the sweeping show by the critics' darling, Forrest Gump.But life ever since has been very kind to this film, and both critics & viewers have embraced its uplifting story of hope & friendship with remarkable amount of respect, love & kindness. Today, The Shawshank Redemption enjoys a position that's arguably even higher than the two classics which eclipsed it back in 1994 and while it was discarded at its time of release, it is now rightly & universally acknowledged as one of the greatest films of all time.The Shawshank Redemption tells the story of Andy Dufresne, a successful banker, who is wrongfully convicted of murdering his wife & her illicit lover and is ultimately sentenced to two consecutive life terms in prison where his coping with the brutal hardships of confined life slowly earns him the respect of his fellow inmates & prison staff, including that of "Red" in whom Andy finds a trusted ally. The remainder of the film explores their friendship over the next two decades.Written & directed by Frank Darabont, this prison drama is a simple but profoundly moving tale of hope, friendship & redemption that'll manage to connect deeply with most of us in one way or another plus it also marks Darabont's directional debut and he couldn't have asked for a better start. All this film has is men in either prison or police uniforms talking to one another over the course of its runtime and yet it never looked dull or felt like dragging at any given moment.Cinematography exquisitely captures the monotonous daily life inside prison and provides considerable depth & realism to the era this film is set in. Every moment of despair has a shadowy appearance while moments of hope gleam with light. Editing is spectacular too as the gradual progression of Andy's life, his friendship with Red, and his determination to not give in to the four walls containing him is effectively unfolded. And Thomas Newman's score beautifully blends with the film's tone & characters' lives, and is emotionally fulfilling.Coming to the performances, Tim Robbins delivers a swashbuckling performance as Andy Dufresne, the banker wrongfully convicted for the crime he didn't commit. And if Robbins is at his best, then Morgan Freeman is even better as Red, Andy's friend who is also serving a life sentence & is notorious amongst the inmates for he can smuggle goods into the prison. Freeman also narrates the story to us at which he does an even better job. His work is grounded & can go easily unnoticed, but the character of Red is the soul of this story.There is a reason why this film still connects with so many people & why many of them have latched on to it. There is a reason why even after two decades, its legacy keeps flourishing & viewers keep returning to it despite its low entertainment value. One major reason is that even though The Shawshank Redemption is a prison drama, its story of imprisonment goes far beyond the bricks & steel rods of a jail house. The entire picture is a reflection of our own imprisonment in the institutions of our daily lives; institutions like work, family, society etc & living up to the expectations of each one of them.On an overall scale, The Shawshank Redemption stresses that based on the outlook of life, there are only two types of people: one who can be free even in prison while others who find themselves imprisoned even in freedom. The message it is trying to resonate is clear: Fear can hold you prisoner, Hope can set you free. And if we all give ourselves some hope, there is nothing we can't survive. Yes, it all seems preachy n everything, but then if there's ever been a motion picture that has earned this sort of right, it's The Shawshank Redemption. Strongly recommended.

review_title: Finally found the reason for depressed life
review_text: Different people may have different feelings when watching the same film. For me, who is unable to change the status quo at present, the deepest feeling after watching this film is that talent and perseverance are the best way for anyone to get freedom under any circumstances.The young banker in the film, with his mastery of bank financial knowledge, not only won his own safety and a little freedom in prison, but also won material and spiritual benefits for his cellmates. It is also because of his mastery of finance that the hero finally completely defeated the cruel and sinister warden and made himself gain material freedom.On the other hand, look at the unremitting application letters every week for six years, the two application letters every week for N years, the tunnels dug day by day with the stone axe that "I can't dig a tunnel in 600 years", the sewer pipes smashed with stones in the sound of thunder and lightning, and the 500 long smelly sewer that I crawled through while vomiting... All these deeply depict a word: perseverance.Anyone who wants to finally get freedom under the blue sky and white clouds must have these two kinds of talent and perseverance.I finally realized why I am still depressed:First: there is no talent that can hold handsI liked painting when I was a child, but when I grew up, I concentrated on reading sages' books. In the college entrance examination, I never mentioned the paintbrush again.I studied medicine in college, but my medical days were used to learn guitar and read idle books. After work, the guitar doesn't have time to practice, so it's naturally wasted.For a long time, I have practiced calligraphy, seal cutting, sketching, comics, Photoshop, flash, Dreamweaver, gardening, etc. On and off. However, no matter which one I am interested in, it is typical to taste it briefly. Although the reasons for giving up halfway are different, in the end, I failed to adhere to it.So, I'm basically the kind of person who knows a little about everything and can't do anything.Second: no perseveranceIn fact, it can be seen from the above that so many hobbies and so many attempts ended in my giving up halfway. If one can persist for half a year, the results will be very different.I am a typical "aspiring person who always aspires". I have a notebook for writing plans. I don't know if others have such a book. I have to create such a small book, because every time, the plan I make will be updated.In fact, every time I make a plan, I hope I can keep doing it, butKnowing that I am not regular, so after the recent plan was made, I solemnly wrote down at the back of the plan: "I hope I can stick to it for three months" - as a result, a month later, these words made me not have the courage to look ahead when writing a new plan.

review_title: Good but does not deserve the glory.
review_text: The Shawshank Redemption is a good movie. It has a good story and good acting. Though I don 't think that the movie is good enough to be at the top of the 250 list at IMDb. I think that it is a great "prison movie" but it's so similar to other books and movies like Midnight Express or The Escape From Alcatraz. A "prison movie" that is much better but doesn't get the glory and credibility is The Green Mile witch made me more emotional and excited. Compared with The Shawshank Redemption, The Green mile has a better storyline and most important an original prison story.The Shawshank Redemption is about man called Andy who is being wrongly accused for a crime that he didn't do. He was given two life sentences for killing his wife and her lover in cold blood. Therefore he is being sent to Shawshank Prison. Andy learns to adapt to prison life and he meets knew friends, but also enemies. The life in prison is hard and he meets a lot of obstacles as the story goes.As I said earlier, it is a good movie and you should see it if you haven't. However in my opinion it is too unoriginal and safe for the best film in history as many other think. By saying safe I mean that the director could have done something that had made me remember the film. Something out of the ordinary. Instead of the "escape prison" unoriginality. Cause now I think it's just a bland movie.Another thing that I think the movie misses is more fighting and crime. Isn't this a prison? Should it not have any sort of violent behavior? Sure Andy fights of a bunch of enemies in a few short scenes, but I don't think that that's enough. The thing is that Andy's enemies are the only bad guys in the whole movie. At least of what we see in this film. The film could have exploited more violence and crime, but instead we get a nice old man that feeds his bird. Andy's friends are so nice that I sometimes feel like they are workmates instead of committed criminals. When they are out in the yard all convicts are just playing ball and talking like they are having a lunch brake. I don't mean that all prisoners should just fight and swear but it could have least been one fight seen in the yard so you get a bit more of that prison feeling.In conclusion it's a good movie with some flaws. It's has many good scenes. Though in my opinion it fails because of its blandness and unoriginality. They should have put more effort in making something more memorable.Based on my judgment it's a 8/10 and I think that it's a fare rating. Hope. It is the single most powerful human emotion. It can keep you alive, and it can destroy your life. Hope can be the one thing left in a world where everything else is taken from you- and The Shawshank Redemption is the perfect artistic visualization of the tremendous power that hope can have over someone who has lost everything else.The opening scene introduces us to a young and successful banker named Andy Dufresne, and the things that have transpired to destroy his life. We can't help but feel sympathy toward a man who finds out that his wife is having an affair, and then gets convicted for the double homicide of his wife and her lover- when he is innocent of the crime. Taken to Shawshank prison for two life sentences, Andy has had his entire life taken from him in a spiral of terrible events. It only gets worse at the prison, as the brutality of the prison guards is unbridled, and a few inmates make his life hell. However, Andy continually surprises the audience with his resilience and his character finds ways to amaze the inmates, the guards, the warden, and the audience. The story itself is not wholly original or groundbreaking, and there is no 'surprise-ending' or major twists that come out of nowhere to shock the audience. However, it is in the delivery of the story that this film excels beyond all others.Every aspect of this movie compliments the incredible script written by Frank Darabont that was based on Stephen King's novella. The music is a composition of slow-moving and peaceful ballads that bring out just how long-winded a life sentence in prison can be, and how undaunted Andy is by the terrible environment he is in. The cameras move slowly and steadily, repeatedly scanning the prison and also emphasizing the endless span that life in prison truly is. On the artistic side, the movie is something to behold. But ultimately, what brings the entire movie together is the beautifully written and exceptionally delivered narration of Morgan Freeman, playing a fellow inmate named Ellis 'Red' Redding. Not only are we given a view into Andy's character through this man's observations, but we also see how Red himself changes his life as a result of Andy Dufresne.The amazing thing about this film is how every detail in the entire movie somehow contributes to the story on the whole. It takes a few times of viewing before you can really appreciate just how intricate the plot is- how every single moment helps increase the power of the incredible ending sequence. It is not too complex, with many tangents that end up confusing the viewer. Instead, it runs with a simple theme and adds to it with everything that is depicted. The only negative thing I have to say about this movie is that the ending seems a bit drawn out, but by this time you are so enthralled and satisfied as a viewer that it should not pose a problem.A great story, told flawlessly, with a powerful message. There is not a lot more that you could ask for in a movie. Entertaining and inspiring. Deep, yet not complicated. A message delivered with undeniable power, and an excellent movie experience overall. If you have ever felt like everything has been taken from you, then learn from Andy Dufresne. 'There's something inside that they can't get to, that they can't touch. It's yours.' Hope. It can set you free.

review_text: In 1946, a banker named Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is convicted of a double murder, even though he stubbornly proclaims his innocence. He's sentenced to a life term at the Shawshank State Prison in Maine, where another lifer, Ellis Red Redding (Morgan Freeman), picks him as the new recruit most likely to crack under the pressure. The ugly realities of prison life are quickly introduced to Andy: a corrupt warden (Bob Gunton), sadistic guards led by Capt. Byron Hadley (Clancy Brown), and inmates who are little better than animals, willing to use rape or beatings to insure their dominance. But Andy does not crack: he has the hope of the truly innocent, which (together with his smarts) allow him to prevail behind bars. He uses his banking skills to win favor with the warden and the guards, doing the books for Norton's illegal business schemes and keeping an eye on the investments of most of the prison staff. In exchange, he is able to improve the prison library and bring some dignity and respect back to many of the inmates, including Red. review_text: I have read thousands of books, and seen thousands of movies. The cinematography breaks the barriers of present day prejudice, without ever directly referencing them. The concepts presented show us what is within our control, and what is decided for us. The dialogue bears witness to the realities we prefer to ignore, without actually giving us unwanted imagery.Most important of all, the film's climax provides us with a shining example of what we all crave: no matter the challenges we face, hope is the only thing that cannot be taken from us. If we retain hope, we will achieve the redemption that every individual seeks.I don't believe any one story can be given the title of the best of all time. However, this film comes as close as motion pictures can achieve.

The Shawshank Redemption, directed by Frank Darabont, is a timeless masterpiece that explores the themes of hope, friendship, and redemption. The film, based on the novella Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption by Stephen King, tells the story of Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins), a banker who is falsely convicted of the murder of his wife and her lover and sent to Shawshank prison.The film's plot is well-crafted, and it skillfully balances moments of tension and despair with moments of hope and joy. The film's characters are well-developed, and their relationships are deep and nuanced. The chemistry between the two main leads, Andy and Red (Morgan Freeman), is particularly strong, and their friendship forms the heart of the movie.The performances in The Shawshank Redemption are superb. Tim Robbins delivers a subtle and nuanced portrayal of Andy, while Morgan Freeman shines as the wise and world-weary Red. The supporting cast is also excellent, with standout performances from Bob Gunton as the cruel and corrupt warden and William Sadler as the tragic figure of Heywood.The film's cinematography is striking, with its use of shadows, low angles, and close-ups creating a sense of intimacy and claustrophobia that perfectly captures the atmosphere of the prison. The film's score, composed by Thomas Newman, is also outstanding, and it perfectly complements the film's themes and moods.The Shawshank Redemption is a poignant and emotionally resonant film that has stood the test of time. It is a testament to the power of hope and friendship, and it is a reminder that even in the darkest of places, there is always a glimmer of light. It is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates great cinema.

review_title: "Get Busy Living, or Get Busy Dying."
review_text: 1994 was a fantastic year for film. "Pulp Fiction", "Forrest Gump", and "The Lion King" are some of my favorite movies of all time. But this one dwarfs all three of them in comparison. The viewer is left thoroughly engaged throughout the entire picture, and there doesn't seem to be a scene that is out of place. The final act is also one of the most satisfying in history. Beautiful performances by Tim Robbins, Morgan Freeman, and the supporting cast will leave you hanging on every scene.Andy Dufresne (Robbins) is a former banker who is convicted of murdering his wife and a professional golfer after finding out about her having an affair with him, but Andy is an innocent man. He is given two life sentences to be served at Shawshank Prison, where he meets Red (Freeman), a smuggler who is also serving time for murder. What follows is a twenty year long saga of heartbreak, guilt, remorse, and ultimately, as the title of the film suggests, redemption.The appeal is multi-layered. On a surface level, "The Shawshank Redemption" works as a piece of entertainment. The characters are all believable and have depth to them. The vicious prison Warden Norton (Bob Gunton) and his brutish prison guard captain Hadley (Clancy Brown) are despicable villains who are very easy to root against. The pacing of the storytelling is excellent as well, and like I said earlier, the structuring of the scenes never really takes you out of the experience. This is one of the easiest movies to sit down and just watch.But beyond that, "The Shawshank Redemption" also works as a piece of art. A poetic tale of finding one's place in society and within themselves. Some of these things are a bit on the nose, with Brooks (James Whitmore) basically serving as the story's antithesis to Red. On first viewing, one would be mistaken to think that this movie is about Andy and his redemption after being wrongly accused. In actuality, it is Red who is ultimately redeemed through a close friendship with an unorthodox inmate who shows him a brighter and more optimistic side to life. Heck, Red is the one who is narrating and leading us through his life. Anything more would dive into spoiler territory, but I think that it goes to show that this is the kind of movie that can't even be mentioned without the inevitability of discussing deeper themes, character motivations, and visual motifs.This one really deserves its recognition as a pillar of cinema. There isn't a whole lot else to say without sounding redundant and repeating what every other movie critic has said to this point, but if you haven't seen it you definitely owe it to yourself to do so.

But it is these same weaknesses that make the film so strong.

review_text: "The Shawshank Redemption" is nearly poetic, but misses slightly because of its straight-forward telling.  That isn't a flaw really.  It's just that considering some of the powerful human emotions and grandiose spritual scenes displayed, the film could have been legendary.  Still, this film is destined to be a classic and rightfully so.  Stephen King hasn't written another story that was better (Title "Rita Hayworth and the Shawshank Redemption" in the book "Diffrent Seasons" which also contains "The Body" which was made into another great movie, "Stand By Me" starring River Phoenix).  Tim Robbins and especially Morgan Freeman are outstanding.  Drama rarely gets muchs better than this and the solitude of human existence is depressingly displayed here.  Wonderful, wonderful!Oh yeah, Morgan Freeman's explanation for being named "Red" is probably one of the purely humorous things you'll ever hear.

review_text: On Sept. 23, 1994, after a premiere at the Toronto film fest, The Shawshank Redemption hit theaters nationwide. The Morgan Freeman film eventually nabbed seven Oscar nominations. The Hollywood Reporter's original review is below: Castle Rock has tapped into the wellspring of yet another Stephen King novella, from the same collection as Stand by Me. While it seems unlikely that this well-wrought film about hope and friendship in a maximum security prison will do Stand by Me-level business, The Shawshank Redemption should appeal to a mature audience. The marketing challenge will be to lure a mainstream audience to this dark drama starring Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman with, to boot, an enigmatic title.Covering a span of time from 1946 to 1967, Shawshank focuses on the plight of a Maine banker, Andy Dufresne (Robbins), sentenced to two life terms for the murder of his wife and lover. Laconic and a bit chilly, Andy is somewhat of an outcast among the uneducated, macho thugs who make up the main brunt of the prison population.Admittedly, he's not an easy guy to get to know and only comes to enjoy a prison friendship when he makes a deal with the prison black-market supplier, Red (Freeman), to get him a tiny hammer for his rock collection. Red is also an enigma to most of the inmates. He keeps his nose clean and his hopes up even though the parole board routinely denies him pardon, obviously a racial antagonism.While the story roils with some rousing prison-type action and is coarsened by an overpowering sense of frustration, The Shawshank Redemption is really about the unlikely friendship between Andy and Red: Each nurtures the other and serves as a touchstone for keeping their sanity intact.Frank Darabont's writing and direction are generally crisp, but Shawshank is a tough watch and audiences could use some time cut from its 142 minutes.In the lead roles, both Robbins and Freeman are outstanding, layering their performances with snippets of individuality: Their small, daily sustenance's and minor triumphs are wonderfully inspiring.Technical contributions are well-crafted, particularly cinematographer Roger Deakins' forbidding lensing. Filmed in a garrison-like former prison in Mansfield, Ohio, Shawshank is often overwhelming in its depiction of the granite-cold, stony horror of prison life. Most splendid is Thomas Newman's somber score, which, at its best moments, alights with radiant textures and sprightly grace notes, nicely emblematic of the film's central theme.

review_title: The Shawshank Redemption: A Timeless Masterpiece of Hope and the Human Spirit
review_text: The Shawshank Redemption is a film that transcends the boundaries of cinema and becomes an emotional experience about the enduring power of hope. It's not just a movie; it's a life lesson, delicately interwoven into a narrative of friendship, perseverance, and belief in something better.From the moment we meet Andy Dufresne, played flawlessly by Tim Robbins, we are taken on a journey of a man wrongfully imprisoned, navigating the brutal realities of Shawshank State Penitentiary. Yet, through all the cruelty, injustice, and despair, Andy never surrenders his spirit. What makes The Shawshank Redemption truly unforgettable is its unwavering focus on hope-an almost spiritual belief that, even in the darkest of places, the light can find a way.Morgan Freeman's portrayal of Red, a man who has long abandoned the idea of hope, acts as a counterbalance to Andy's quiet optimism. Their friendship is the beating heart of the film, and through Andy's relentless determination, Red begins to rediscover what hope can mean. As Red puts it, "Hope is a dangerous thing," yet by the end of the movie, we learn that hope is also the most powerful thing a person can hold onto.Director Frank Darabont crafts a story that isn't just about breaking out of prison, but breaking free from the mental chains that hold people down. The pacing, the dialogue, the breathtaking score by Thomas Newman-everything builds towards a crescendo that reminds us that hope is not just something to cling to; it's something to fight for.The final scenes are nothing short of cathartic, leaving you with a sense of awe and reflection on the strength of the human spirit. If ever there was a film that illustrates the power of hope to heal, to transform, and to liberate, The Shawshank Redemption is it.Simply put, this film is a masterpiece-10/10. A story that reminds us to "get busy living or get busy dying," but above all, to never stop hoping.

The short novel by Stephen King has been adapted by Owen O'Neill and Dave Johns and is likely to prove popular with fans of the film as well as those who are too young to remember the original format. Based on the 1982 novella Rita Hayworth and The Shawshank Redemption, the play examines desperation, injustice, friendship and hope behind the bars of a maximum security facility. The 1994 feature film, regularly voted Britain's favourite ever movie, starred Tim Robbins and Morgan Freeman and was nominated for seven Academy Awards. Two of TV's best loved leading men, Ian Kelsey (Doctors, Casualty and Emmerdale) and Patrick Robinson (Casualty, Midsomer Murders), star in this new production of The Shawshank Redemption, which is running at Milton Keynes Theatre until Saturday. Incarcerated at the notorious Shawshank facility, he quickly learns that no one can survive alone. However, when Warden Stammas decides to bully Andy into subservience and exploit his talents for accountancy, a desperate plan is quietly hatched. Andy Dufresne (Tim Robbins) is tall, lean, and a very successful Vice President for a bank in Portland, Maine. Andy's wife (Renee Blaine) is a beautiful and slim brunette who finally breaks her silence about her love affair with Glenn Quentin (Scott Mann) a golf pro. She informs Andy that she wants a divorce in Reno which he denied her. Now Andy finds himself facing a judge and jury as he flashes back to a dark and drunken night sitting in a wooden area at the end of a driveway in his car with a trusty bottle of Rosewood liquor in one hand, a musical tone "If I didn't care" (Jack Lawrence) playing in the background as a reaches for his six shooter from the glove compartment. Andy's blank face tells his version of his innocence; however, the neighbors plus two dead bodies tell the other side of the story. The dead body of Andy's wife and the golf pro give him two life sentences in the big houseShawshank Prison!Andy arrives at Shawshank with the same blank facial expression that granted him the bus ride to the prison. As the welcoming committee provided a grand opening to the bus load of "Fresh Fish" inmates. This single file march of leg irons clanking, feet shuffling across the dusty prison yard, as fresh fish pass by the thunderous claps, and yelling voices which intimated some of the new fish. Ellis Boyd "Red" Redding (Morgan Freeman) placed a bet of 10 cigarettes on the new fish named Andy Dufresne. Andy has a naive way of thinking, along with his new normal routine of strolling the prison yard in search of smooth rocks while keeping to himself. Andy finally breaks his silence after a month and engages in a conversation with Red.Andy's life sentence was almost cut short while eavesdropping on a conversation of the brutal Captain Hadley (Clancy Brown). Since Andy befriends Red and his crew of intimates Brooks Hatlen (James Whitmore), Heywood (William Sadler), Jigger (Neil Giuntoli), Floyd (Brian Libby), and Skeet (Larry Brandenburg), he placed a request for a bottle of suds after the rigged roof job is completed by this team of inmates. Andy was able to do his "Real Job" again by performing banking services for every prison guard in Shawshank. Although he longed for this new freedom Andy still has to fight off his predator Boggs Diamond (Mark Rolston).Andy is on the verge of losing his freedom due to his overzealous attitude toward Warden Norton (Bob Gunton). The Warden provides Andy with a few options while he spends two months in solitary confinement to reset his mind and his mouth. This melodramatic crime film will have your emotions racing as you cook up a new avenue for Andy to travel down.The actors in "The Shawshank Redemption" have a more boisterous tone compared to the relaxed spoken actors in "The Green Mile" John Coffey (Michael Clark Duncan), Paul Edgecomb (Tom Hanks), Brutus "Brutal" Howell (David Morse), "Wild Bill" Wharton (Sam Rockwell), Eduard Delacroix (Michael Jeter), and Dean Stanton (Barry Pepper). The lighting for these two melodramatic crime films are different. Both John Coffey and Andy Dufresne are in prison for murder. Andy has more of a dark shadow over his face at times probably due to depression and when harm is coming his way. The lighting changes for him when he is able to accomplish a "normal / human" side of his past. John Coffey has a brighter atmosphere when is able to arouse those around him to think outside the box and have a more positive attitude in their heart toward life. John and Andy have to figure out which way to go in order to have freedom while in prison.

THE SHAWSHANK REDEMPTION is a kind of morality tale that is definitely one of Stephen King's more restrained kind of stories, dealing mostly with a character study of two individuals sharing imprisonment and the consequences that await them when the tale ends.TIM ROBBINS is a man wrongly convicted of murder and serving a long prison term while MORGAN FREEMAN (who plays the narrator with great dignity) describes himself as "the only guilty man in Shawshank." The hardships of prison life are captured in brief scenes that make the viewer wish that Robbins will find a way of escape.Along the way, he is gang raped by prisoners and treated harshly by a brutal warden and some of his spirit seems to vanish. But Robbins is quietly effective as a prisoner who makes a good adjustment when he takes charge of the prison library and sees to it that there's a wider selection of books than the kind of potboilers that King is noted for writing. A touch of irony here, no? The closing scenes are a bit of a stretch and a reminder of just who wrote this prison tale--but still, they make an impact because of all that happens before.It's a bittersweet story, a sort of horrific fairy-tale of what might have happened, but the viewer will be caught up in the story because of the tremendously skillful story-telling magic of Stephen King and director Frank Darabont who also wrote the screenplay.
